Abstract 45

Photodiodes based on two-dimensional semiconductors are of potential use in the 46

development of optoelectronic devices, but their photovoltaic efficiency is limited by strong 47

Fermi level pinning at metal–semiconductor contacts. Typical metal–interlayer–semiconductor 48

contacts can address this issue, but can also lead to an increase in series resistance. Here, we 49

report a conductive-bridge interlayer contact that offers both Fermi level depinning and low 50

resistance. We create an oxide interlayer that decouples the metal and semiconductor, while 51

embedded gold nanoclusters in the interlayer act as conductive paths that facilitate efficient 52

charge transport. Using these contacts, we fabricate a tungsten disulfide (WS2) photodiode with 53

a photoresponsivity of 0.29 A W–1, linear dynamic range of 122 dB, and power conversion 54

efficiency of 9.9%. Our approach also provides a platform for probing photocarrier dynamics, 55

and we find that contact recombination substantially impacts photovoltaic performance. In 56

addition, we illustrate the potential of using photodiodes with these conductive-bridge 57

interlayer contacts as full-colour 2D and 3D imagers. 58

Main 60

Photodiodes are widely used for light detection, harvesting, and emitting applications1. By 61

scaling the devices to nanometre scales, it is possible to improve their operational speed, power 62

efficiency, and integration density2. Layered two-dimensional (2D) transition metal 63

dichalcogenides are expected to be ideal candidates for the absorber materials in miniaturized 64

photodiodes because of their atomically uniform thickness and strong light–matter 65

interactions3–5. However, many photodiodes based on 2D transition metal dichalcogenides 66

suffer from low photovoltaic efficiency (power conversion efficiencies are typically less than 67

5%)6,7 and a limited operating range, primarily due to inefficient charge collection at the 68

electrical contacts. 69

One of the fundamental parameters that determine charge-collection efficiency is the Schottky 70

barrier height at metal–semiconductor contacts1,8. Ideally, by careful selection of the contact 71

metal, the Schottky barrier for photogenerated carriers (electrons and holes) can be made 72

sufficiently low to facilitate charge transport in and out of an optoelectronic device. However, 73

in reality, an ideal Schottky barrier is not formed due to interface phenomena at metal–2D 74

semiconductor junctions, such as metal-induced gap states (MIGS) and defect-induced gap 75

states (DIGS) (Fig. 1a(i)), leading to strong Fermi level pinning (FLP)8–11. This pinning, 76

regardless of the metal work function (WF), usually results in a large Schottky barrier at the 77

contacts, which severely hampers charge collection and consequently the performance of 2D 78

photovoltaic devices12,13. Although various approaches to mitigate FLP have been proposed, 79

such as creating van der Waals (vdW) contacts via metal transfer8,12 or using 2D vdW metal 80

contacts9, these techniques have a limited choice of transferrable metals and transfer-process- 81

related issues that can increase the cost and complexity of device fabrication. 82

An alternative method to avoid this problem is to create a metal–interlayer–semiconductor 83


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

(MIS) contact14–16 (Fig. 1a(ii)). Introducing an interlayer to decouple the interactions between 84

the metal and semiconductor can potentially prevent FLP, thus enabling precise control over 85

the Schottky barrier and thus the charge-collection efficiency of optoelectronic devices. But so 86

far the MIS approach has yielded limited success, primarily owing to the extreme sensitivity 87

of tunnelling to the interlayer thickness: even a sub-nanometre increase in the interlayer 88

thickness (and in the tunnelling width) causes an undesirable high series resistance17,18. This 89

high series resistance is problematic as it severely limits the dynamic sensing range and 90

photovoltaic performance of the device17, especially under intense illumination. In addition, 91

depositing an extremely thin interlayer on 2D surfaces with high uniformity is technically 92

challenging. 93

In this Article, we report a method, which we term conductive-bridge interlayer contact (CBIC) 94

(Fig. 1a(iii)), to form low-resistance and pinning-free interlayer contacts. The method 95

incorporates gold atoms into an oxide interlayer, creating conductive pathways within the 96

interlayer. These pathways can substantially reduce the series resistance induced by the 97

interlayer, thus providing low-resistance contacts without the trade-off problem typically 98

encountered in conventional MIS contacts17,18. We use CBIC contacts to create a tungsten 99

disulfide (WS2) Schottky photodiode that exhibits good photovoltaic performance over a wide 100

operating dynamic range. The CBIC is also a useful platform to explore photocarrier dynamics, 101

unveiling that contact recombination associated with the Schottky barrier greatly impacts the 102

performance of 2D photovoltaics. Finally, we demonstrate full-colour 2D and 3D imaging 103

using prototype CBIC-integrated image sensors. 104

Architecture design of the CBIC 106

*Figure 1b shows a schematic of pre-patterned CBIC fabrication via sequential sputtering. First, 107*


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

a low-WF metal (Al, Ti, Cr, Cu; ~20 nm thick) and Au (1 nm nominal thickness) were 108

sequentially deposited on a SiO2 substrate without breaking vacuum. Note that the addition of 109

a trace amount of Au during the sputtering process is crucial in this design (Supplementary 110

Figs. 1 and 2), as further discussed later. Afterwards, the as-deposited metal layer was exposed 111

to ambient atmosphere to form an approximately 5 nm thick oxidization layer on the surface 112

of the metal, as confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements 113

(Supplementary Fig. 3). This oxide layer serves as a physical spacer that decouples the metal– 114

semiconductor interaction, thereby suppressing FLP16. Finally, the resulting CBIC electrode 115

was used to fabricate a vertical Schottky diode structure, in which multilayer WS2 (~50 nm) 116

was used as the absorber, and the CBIC and chlorine-doped SnSe2 (Cl–SnSe2, ~10 nm) were 117

used as bottom and top electrodes, respectively. The Cl–SnSe2 employed here not only offers 118

ideal band alignment with multilayer WS2 but also serves as a transparent conductive electrode 119

that enables top illumination operation. The material properties of Cl–SnSe2 are provided in 120

Supplementary Figs. 4–6. Figure 1c presents a schematic illustration and optical image of a 121

complete device (see Supplementary Fig. 7 for AFM measurements of the sample thicknesses). 122

We first performed electrical characterization of a CBIC made from Al, hereafter referred to 123

as CBIC–Al, using conductive atomic force microscopy (CAFM). For simplicity, we mostly 124

focus on CBIC–Al as an example in our discussions. Two different samples were prepared and 125

measured for comparison, one with the addition of elemental Au and the other without, as 126

illustrated in Fig. 1d,e. The currents recorded as the CAFM tip (applied constant bias of 1 V) 127

scanned across the samples are presented in Fig. 1f,g. A sharp contrast was found, where the 128

CBIC–Al with Au structure shows multiple conductive spots across the entire sample, with an 129

abrupt current increase (Fig. 1f; see also Supplementary Fig. 8 for basic information such as 130

size and density), whereas CBIC–Al without Au shows no noticeable current change (Fig. 1g). 131


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

This observed distinction clearly suggests the existence of electrical conduction paths within 132

the oxide interlayer of CBIC–Al with Au. Cross-sectional scanning transmission electron 133

microscopy (STEM) measurement followed to directly probe the conducting path in a complete 134

device of CBIC–Al/WS2/Cl–SnSe2 (the same device as in Fig. 1c). A typical cross-sectional 135

STEM image clearly revealed multiple Au nanoclusters (approximately 2 nm in diameter) 136

uniformly embedded within the amorphous AlOx interlayer (Fig. 1h,i), which is further 137

supported by an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping image (Supplementary 138

*Fig. 9). Most probably, electrical conduction across the interlayer primarily occurs via the Au- 139*

induced gap states, as evidenced by XPS measurement and density functional theory (DFT) 140

calculations (Supplementary Fig. 10). The coupling between elemental Au atoms and the AlOx 141

layer can induce finite gap states within the bandgap. Consequently, unoccupied gap states near 142

the Fermi level may contribute to efficient charge-carrier transport through the interlayer, 143

which could be responsible for the observed enhanced conductance in CBIC–Al. Note that this 144

operational mechanism differs markedly from that of a conventional MIS contact, which 145

strongly relies on tunnelling transport (Supplementary Fig. 11). It is also observed that the 146

WS2/Cl–SnSe2 interface features an atomically clean contact without apparent disorder 147

(Supplementary Fig. 12). Taken together, the data in Fig. 1 demonstrate that the incorporation 148

of a small amount of Au into the interlayer establishes robust electrical conduction pathways 149

that improve the conductivity of the CBIC. As we show below, these conductive pathways 150

effectively reduce contact resistance in the CBIC, which in turn facilitates charge extraction in 151

2D optoelectronic devices. 152

Characterizations of the CBIC 154

One intriguing feature of the CBIC method is its versatility with various metals. This allows 155


<!-- Page 8 -->


8

for the tunability of work functions, which is crucial for the rational design and fabrication of 156

electronics. To demonstrate that the WF of the CBIC can be tailored simply by changing the 157

metal type, we characterized CBICs made from different metals with varying WFs (Ti, Cr, and 158

Cu) following the identical process as with CBIC–Al. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) 159

was used to evaluate the WF distributions of the CBICs; all KPFM images exhibit highly 160

uniform features over a large area (Fig. 2a), indicating electrical homogeneity of the CBICs. 161

The measured WF values of the CBICs were essentially similar to those of pristine metal 162

films8,19, as shown in Fig. 2b. The mean WFs were found to be 3.92 ± 0.04 eV for CBIC–Al, 163

4.12 ± 0.05 eV for CBIC–Ti, 4.36 ± 0.02 eV for CBIC–Cr, and 4.74 ± 0.04 eV for CBIC–Cu. 164

This result suggests that the WF of the CBIC is largely dictated by the underlying deposited 165

metal, highlighting the versatility of this method. Slight deviations from the intrinsic WFs are 166

likely caused by possible interfacial alloying between metals20 or interfacial dipoles at the 167

metal–semiconductor junctions21. As shown in topographical AFM images, the surface 168

roughness of the CBICs was negligibly different, with root mean square (RMS) values ranging 169

from 0.56 to 0.69 nm (Supplementary Fig. 13). We additionally performed XPS and Raman 170

spectroscopy to investigate the chemical states of the CBIC–Al/WS2 interface. Here, we 171

intentionally prepared the sample using thin WS2 (~2.86 nm, four layers) to ensure a reliable 172

evaluation of the interfacial chemistry (Supplementary Fig. 14). The XPS spectrum obtained 173

from CBIC–Al/WS2 (Fig. 2c) is almost identical to that of pristine WS2. Also, non- 174

stoichiometric WxSy peaks were not observed, suggesting that the WS2 layer remained largely 175

intact without any chemical perturbation. The Raman spectrum (Supplementary Fig. 14d) also 176

shows no peaks associated with non-stoichiometric WxSy, further confirming that CBIC–Al in 177

contact with WS2 does not introduce any chemical reactions, defects, or strain at the interface 178

or within the WS2. 179


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

With minimized interface disorders on the 2D semiconductor, the CBIC can effectively 180

suppress FLP originating from DIGS22. Additionally, decoupling the metal–2D semiconductor 181

interaction by the interlayer can greatly suppress the MIGS that strongly pin the Fermi level10. 182

To demonstrate this, we fabricated top-gated WS2 transistors with CBICs as source and drain 183

electrodes and investigated their contact properties using temperature-dependent charge 184

transport measurements (see Methods for details about the device fabrication). Figure 2d shows 185

a schematic (upper) and optical image (lower) of a top-gated WS2 transistor fabricated with 186

CBICs. As shown in Fig. 2e–h, all devices with CBICs exhibited similar n-type characteristics, 187

regardless of the CBIC type (room temperature I–V characteristics of the same devices are 188

shown in Supplementary Fig. 15). However, both CBIC–Cr and CBIC–Cu devices exhibited a 189

much stronger temperature dependence of current compared to CBIC–Al and CBIC–Ti devices, 190

indicating high Schottky barriers at the CBIC–Cr and CBIC–Cu contacts. In particular, the 191

CBIC–Cu device with a relatively high WF exhibited an ambipolar behaviour, with nearly 192

symmetric p- and n-branches (see Supplementary Fig. 15d for a log-scale plot). The 193

reproducibility of this behaviour was also verified with another five CBIC–Cu devices all 194

fabricated with similar device geometries (Supplementary Fig. 16). A statistical analysis of 195

carrier polarity, threshold voltage (VT), and electron field-effect mobility (μe) for different 196

CBIC types of the aforementioned devices is shown in Fig. 2i. Here, the carrier polarity was 197

characterized by the current ratio of I5V (IDS at VGS = 5 V) to I−5V (IDS at VGS = –5 V), which 198

represents the majority carrier type. As the WF of the CBIC increased, a clear transition in the 199

majority charge carrier was observed along with an increased VT. The observed trend of WF 200

dependence can be attributed to a highly tunable Schottky barrier height due to Fermi level 201

depinning, which is consistent with previous studies8. Significant degradation in μe was 202

observed in both CBIC–Cr and CBIC–Cu devices, due to their large electron barriers8,23. 203


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

To gain insight into the observed distinctions resulting from different CBIC types, we further 204

estimated the Schottky barrier height (SBH) using temperature-dependent I–V measurements24. 205

A detailed description of SBH extraction can be found in Supplementary Fig. 17. Plots of 206

effective barrier ΦB versus VGS for the different CBICs are presented in Fig. 2j along with the 207

2D Cl–SnSe2 contact exploited in this work. The SBH (ΦSB) for each contact was determined 208

under the flat band condition (VGS = VFB) and plotted against the metal WF (Fig. 2k). For the 209

CBICs, the SBH value was highly dependent on the CBIC work functions. The pinning factor 210

(S = |dΦSB/dW|) was calculated to be 1.17, largely following the Schottky–Mott rule (S = 1), 211

which clearly indicates the Fermi level depinning effect. This contrasts with direct 212

metallization samples, all fabricated by electron beam evaporation (Supplementary Fig. 17). 213

The absence of pinning can be ascribed to an effective suppression of MIGS25 and/or DIGS26, 214

provided by minimized metal–semiconductor interaction. We further confirmed that this 215

depinning effect is also valid for ultrathin WS2 (monolayer and bilayer) devices, as shown in 216

Supplementary Fig. 18. Additionally, for the device with Cl–SnSe2, we observed p-type 217

behaviour, with a hole SBH of 317 meV, consistent with the Schottky−Mott rule and its field- 218

effect transistor characteristics (Supplementary Fig. 19). The above results demonstrate the 219

versatility and pinning-free characteristics of the CBIC, which are key prerequisites for 220

efficient 2D optoelectronic devices. Below, by fabricating 2D Schottky photodiodes, we reveal 221

unique advantages and the potential of the CBIC. 222

CBIC-based WS2 diode as a photodetector 224

The CBIC can be employed to fabricate a 2D photodetector that exhibits a robust 225

photodetection ability, including a large linear dynamic range (LDR), high responsivity, and 226

fast photoresponse. Figure 3a illustrates a schematic of our designed vertical WS2 Schottky 227


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

diode (top) and the energy-level alignment of the materials (bottom) considered in this study. 228

In principle, the WF of the electron-selective (hole-selective) contact should be aligned with 229

the conduction (valence) band of the absorber layer to facilitate efficient extraction of 230

photogenerated carriers. We first explored this picture experimentally by measuring a device 231

fabricated with palladium metal (Pd) as hole-selective contacts. The device showed poor 232

rectifying behaviour (Fig. 3b) due to severe FLP near the conduction band edge of WS2. To 233

solve this issue, we adopted 2D Cl–SnSe2 metal as a pinning-free electrode, as previously 234

reported9. As shown in Fig. 3c,d, the Cl–SnSe2-contacted devices exhibited clear rectification 235

behaviour, with high on/off current ratios exceeding 104. To ensure satisfactory performance, 236

we applied Cl–SnSe2 as hole-selective contacts throughout the remainder of this study unless 237

otherwise specified. 238

Compared with MIS devices, CBIC devices generally exhibited better rectification, largely 239

due to an increased on-current (Fig. 3e). This observation suggests that electrical conduction 240

through the conductive paths of the CBIC is the primary factor responsible for the improved 241

charge injection and the resulting higher on-current, as compared to MIS devices. No 242

significant difference in rectification was observed between CBIC–Ti and MIS–Ti devices, 243

probably owing to a sufficiently low interfacial barrier of the TiOx interlayer (Supplementary 244

*Fig. 20). Under visible light illumination (532 nm), the Schottky diode with CBIC–Al 245*

demonstrated a clear photoresponse, in which the photocurrent (Iph) linearly increased with 246

light intensity, exhibiting light-sensing capability (Fig. 3f). A very broad photocurrent plateau 247

was also observed at a bias ranging from 0 V to –1.5 V, which is crucial for stable photodetector 248

operation27. The spectral responsivity of the same device was also measured, revealing that the 249

photoresponse follows the absorption spectrum of the WS2/Cl–SnSe2 heterostructure 250

(Supplementary Fig. 21). 251


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

Besides light-sensing capability, a large dynamic range with excellent linearity is of great 252

importance for practical applications and successful commercialization of 2D photodetectors. 253

The majority of previous investigations have mainly focused on reporting the responsivity of 254

devices at a specific illumination condition—note that a high photoconductive gain of a device 255

under specific light intensities does not necessarily indicate superior light detection capability 256

due to photogating effects28,29—while relatively few studies have attempted to evaluate the 257

device LDR, defined as the range of linear responsivity under different light intensities30,31. 258

Moreover, even less attention has been paid to device performance under intense illumination 259

above 100 mW cm−2, which indeed resembles the operating conditions of real applications. 260

*Figure 3g plots the photocurrent at V = 0 V (photovoltaic mode) as a function of incident light 261*

power. Our device exhibited an excellent linearity from the lowest detectable limit, 262

4.3 μW cm−2, to 5.4 W cm−2, corresponding to an LDR of 122 dB, which outperforms 263

previously reported 2D photodetectors (Supplementary Table 1) at a similar wavelength and 264

achieves comparable performance to commercial photodetectors (Si or InGaAs)32,33. Most 265

importantly, evidence for the effectiveness of the CBIC in reducing the series resistance of the 266

contacts is shown in Fig. 3h. Compared with MIS devices, the CBIC devices generally featured 267

a higher LDR (100–126 dB, Supplementary Figs. 22 and 23). Owing to the substantial 268

reduction in series resistance, photodetection at higher light levels becomes possible, thereby 269

extending the photodetection range and leading to an enhanced LDR (further discussion is 270

provided in Supplementary Fig. 24). We also observed a nearly consistent responsivity (R) of 271

~0.29 A W−1 and a specific detectivity (D*) of ~2.11 × 1010 cm Hz1/2 W−1 over a wide 272

photodetection range spanning six orders of magnitude (Fig. 3i, and see Supplementary Fig. 25 273

for the frequency-dependent noise power spectral density). Frequency response measurement 274

(Fig. 3j) revealed a fast response of the device with a 3 dB bandwidth of > 100 kHz, which is 275


<!-- Page 13 -->


13

beyond the bandwidth limit of our instrument set-up (Supplementary Fig. 26). Simultaneously, 276

we obtained a fast response time of less than 5 μs (Fig. 3j, inset), agreeing well with the 277

measured –3 dB cutoff frequency. We believe that the response speed can be further improved 278

by reducing the carrier transit time and minimizing device resistance and capacitance, as 279

reported previously2,34. Photoswitching behaviours at modulated frequencies (100 Hz and 1 280

kHz) are shown in Supplementary Fig. 27. Additionally, the CBIC approach can also be 281

extended to other 2D semiconductors, including ReS2, MoS2, and WSe2 (Supplementary Fig. 282

28). Similar to the WS2 devices, all these devices exhibited a clear photoresponse, 283

demonstrating the universality of the CBIC method. 284

CBIC-based WS2 diode as a photovoltaic cell 286

In addition to photodetection, CBIC-based WS2 Schottky diodes can be operated as 287

photovoltaic cells, as illustrated in Fig. 4a. Figure 4b shows an optical image of a CBIC–Al 288

device along with corresponding spatial-resolution photocurrent mapping (at V = 0 V), 289

measured with a 532 nm laser spot scanned over the device. The strongest photocurrent was 290

observed to occur only in the heterojunction, suggesting that the photoresponse of our device 291

originates from the photovoltaic effect. Figure 4c compares representative J–V characteristics 292

between CBIC–Al and control MIS–Al devices, measured under 532 nm laser with a power of 293

44 mW cm−2. Compared to the MIS–Al device, the CBIC–Al device exhibited much improved 294

performance with a fill factor (FF) of 54% and an open-circuit voltage (VOC) of ~0.66 V, 295

yielding a high power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 9.91%; this value is notably comparable 296

to or higher than previous 2D semiconductor Schottky or p–n photodiodes (Supplementary 297

*Table 2). We further note that devices with other CBICs also demonstrated similarly enhanced 298*

performance compared to the control MIS device (see Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30 for more 299


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

details on the CBIC and MIS devices, respectively). The noticeable enhancement in PCE 300

primarily arises from a substantially increased FF, as follows: the relatively high conductivity 301

of the CBIC can substantially reduce electron extraction resistance to enhance the FF. Long- 302

term stability was also assessed, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 31. After one month of storage 303

in ambient environments, the CBIC–Al device did not exhibit such a high PCE (less than 1%) 304

due to interfacial oxidation. Nevertheless, by employing subsequent encapsulation or other 305

measure, high photovoltaic performance with air stability can potentially be achieved in the 306

future. 307

With the capability to control the WF, our CBIC approach offers a versatile platform for both 308

fundamental photophysics studies and high-performance photovoltaic devices. Although 309

significant progress has been made in other photovoltaic technologies16 (such as silicon, 310

perovskite, and organic photovoltaics) through modulation of the WF in electrodes, this aspect 311

has not yet been investigated in 2D electronics due to the lack of a suitable contact architecture 312

that simultaneously offers versatile WF control and a pinning-free nature. To obtain a statistical 313

variation of device performance, we measured 28 devices all fabricated with similar geometries; 314

the photovoltaic parameters of the corresponding devices are summarized in Fig. 4d. A clear 315

and distinguishable trend shows that both VOC and FF strongly decreased with increasing WF 316

of the CBIC. For example, when the WF increased from ~3.9 eV to ~4.7 eV, the average VOC 317

(FF) decreased from 0.7 V (60%) to 0.4 V (30%). This WF dependency was more pronounced 318

at high illumination intensities, which can be confirmed by light-intensity-dependent 319

measurements. In Fig. 4e, for two contrasting contacts (namely, CBIC–Al and –Cu) we plot 320

VOC as a function of light intensity. For the CBIC–Cu device with a relatively high WF 321

(~4.7 eV), VOC showed saturation behaviour with increasing light intensity. In contrast, for the 322

CBIC–Al device with a low WF (~3.9 eV), VOC increased continuously with light intensity, 323


<!-- Page 15 -->


15

with a constant ideality factor (n) of ~1.27, indicative of Shockley–Read–Hall recombination35. 324

In addition, the FF degradation trends were identical but to different extents, where the trend 325

correlated with the magnitude of the WF of the CBIC electrode (Fig. 4f). 326

Since both VOC and FF are closely associated with nonradiative recombination17,36, the 327

observed trend can be explained by the effect of contact recombination resulting from the 328

Schottky barrier at contacts36,37, as illustrated by the simulated band diagrams in Fig. 4g,h. For 329

the CBIC–Cu device under light illumination (Fig. 4g), the high SBH (ΦSB ≈ 840 meV) could 330

block some of the photogenerated electrons, increasing the probability of non-collected carriers 331

undergoing carrier recombination near the contacts. This reduces the quasi-Fermi-level 332

splitting and charge-collection efficiency, thereby limiting both VOC and FF. In contrast, for the 333

CBIC–Al device under light illumination (Fig. 4h), photogenerated electrons can readily 334

overcome the contact barrier (ΦSB ≈ 20 meV) and reach the collecting electrode before carrier 335

recombination occurs, which leads to enhancement in both VOC and FF (further details are given 336

in Supplementary Fig. 32). To corroborate this interpretation, we performed numerical 337

simulations using a drift-diffusion model (details are provided in Supplementary Table 3). For 338

a reliable comparison, we used identical material parameters except for the WF of the electrode 339

(3.92 eV versus 4.74 eV). As shown in Fig. 4e, our simulated data quantitatively matched the 340

experimental data for VOC. This result is also in accordance with the calculated contact 341

recombination current (Supplementary Fig. 33), where contact recombination predominantly 342

contributed to the total recombination current in the CBIC–Cu device with a high WF. Taken 343

together, these results highlight the importance of contact recombination reduction in 344

enhancing the efficiency of 2D photovoltaics. 345

Full-colour 3D imaging demonstration 347


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

Fast response speed and high detectivity to visible light make our CBIC-integrated photodiodes 348

promising for full-colour imaging applications. To demonstrate this, we employed a CBIC–Al- 349

integrated WS2 photodiode as a full-colour (RGB, red/green/blue) image sensor to build a 3D 350

imaging system as an alternative to commercially available imagers. 3D integral imaging, a 351

promising technique for 3D visualization, captures depth information by using an array of 352

microlenses that allows for the recording of multiple perspectives of a scene to create a realistic 353

3D image38,39. This approach eliminates the need for a specialized viewing device for depth 354

perception, which is advantageous compared to other 3D imaging methods. Figure 5a 355

illustrates the principle of the 3D integral imaging system, involving two major processes: a 356

pickup process and a reconstruction process. In the pickup process, an image sensor captures 357

light reflected off an object or objects from different perspectives, resulting in sub-images 358

referred to as elemental images. Then in the reconstruction process, these elemental images are 359

reconstructed into a 3D image using a lens array. 360

Our full-colour 3D integral imaging set-up is schematically illustrated in Fig. 5b. While 361

previous imaging demonstrations have mainly relied on transmissive-type systems30,39–41, often 362

constrained by limited photoresponsivity in low-light conditions, we employ a reflective-type 363

imaging system where a CBIC-integrated image sensor captures reflected light from objects 364

illuminated by a light source, which is crucial for practical applications. For this study, the 365

object was illuminated with white light at an intensity of ~1,000 lux, corresponding to office 366

illumination conditions42. The light reflected from the object passes through the camera lens 367

and is irradiated onto the CBIC–Al image sensor. The photocurrent of the device is then 368

recorded with an external source meter. To obtain full-colour images, a series of scanning 369

operations were conducted at various wavelengths (650 nm for red, 550 nm for green, and 370

450 nm for blue) using an optical bandpass filter. Because the proposed CBIC-integrated 2D 371


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

devices have a broadband photovoltaic response and excellent linearity of photoresponsivity in 372

low-light conditions, fast, full-colour, and high-quality image processing becomes feasible with 373

the reflective-type imaging system. A photograph of the imaging system is shown in 374

Supplementary Fig. 34, and further information on the experiment is provided in 375

Supplementary Table 4, and Methods. 376

Conclusion 406

We have reported a conductive-bridge interlayer method for creating low-resistance and 407

pinning-free contacts. The contacts consist of an oxide interlayer embedded with gold 408

nanoclusters, which creates conductive pathways that enable efficient charge transport across 409

the interlayer. WS2 Schottky photodiodes with CBIC contacts showed a good photovoltaic 410

performance over a wide dynamic operating range. We also apply this technique to investigate 411

the photocarrier dynamics at the contacts, revealing how the Schottky barrier at the contacts 412

determines the photovoltaic performance. Finally, we demonstrated full-colour 2D and 3D 413

imaging using CBIC-integrated photodiodes. Our study achieves low-resistance and pinning- 414

free contacts for efficient optoelectronic devices, and establishes an approach for making 415

metal–interlayer–semiconductor contacts that could be generally applied to various metals with 416

high work functions. 417

Methods 419

CBIC fabrication. Electron-beam lithography (EBL) was used to pattern the CBIC electrodes. 420

After developing the resist, low-WF metal (20 nm; Al, Ti, Cr, Cu) and Au (nominal 1 nm) were 421

sequentially deposited using sputtering without breaking vacuum. Subsequently, to obtain a 422

dense native oxide interlayer, the samples were naturally oxidized in ambient atmosphere for 423

more than 3 h. Finally, the samples were lifted off with acetone and rinsed in isopropanol. 424

Synthesis of Cl–SnSe2. Cl–SnSe2 (SnSe1.98Cl0.02) was synthesized via chemical vapour 425

transport, following a procedure described elsewhere44. In brief, powders of Sn, Se, and SnCl2 426

were mixed in stoichiometric proportions and loaded into a furnace. The reaction [(2 − x)Sn + 427

xSnCl2 + 2(2 − x)Se → 2SnSe2−xClx] was performed via a two-step process: the mixture was 428

heated to 250 °C for 24 h and then annealed at 400 °C for 48 h. Finally, the sample was melted 429

at 750 °C for 24 h and slowly cooled to room temperature. 430

Device fabrication and measurements. For photodiode fabrication, we first loaded a pre- 431

patterned CBIC onto a SiO2 substrate. Using poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) films, WS2 (40– 432

50 nm) and Cl–SnSe2 (5–10 nm) were sequentially transferred onto the pre-patterned CBIC 433

using a micromanipulator. Subsequently, Ti/Au layers (1 nm/30 nm) were patterned and 434

deposited using sputtering to serve as contact pads for electrical measurements. Photocurrent 435

was measured under ambient conditions using an Agilent 4156C parameter analyser both in 436

the dark and under illumination by diode lasers (Thorlabs). The light intensity was adjusted 437

using neutral density filters in the beam path and calibrated with a commercial Si photodetector. 438

The LDR was calculated as follows: LDR = 20 log(𝑃𝑃high/𝑃𝑃low) , where Phigh and Plow 439

represent the highest and lowest light power at which the measured photocurrent of the device 440

exhibits a linear relation with the light power. Transient response and photoelectrical bandwidth 441


<!-- Page 20 -->


20

measurements were made with a high-speed oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS2024) coupled with 442

a function generator (Tektronix AFG31000). 443

Fabrication of the top-gated CBIC-contacted transistors was similar to that of the photodiode 444

devices. WS2 (40–50 nm), h-BN (15–20 nm), and graphite (10–20 nm) were exfoliated onto 445

PDMS films and subsequently transferred onto a pre-patterned CBIC, which served as both 446

source and drain electrodes. Finally, gate metallization was performed similarly as for the 447

photodiode devices. For the evaporated contact devices, a Ti (1 nm)/Au (10 nm) local bottom 448

gate was first prepared on a SiO2 substrate as the back-gate electrode. Afterward, h-BN (15– 449

20 nm) and multilayer WS2 flakes (40–50 nm) were transferred on top of the pre-deposited gate 450

electrodes. Finally, the metal electrodes (20-nm-thick metal capped with 50-nm-thick Au to 451

prevent reaction between metal and ambient oxygen and water) were defined using electron 452

beam lithography followed by electron beam evaporation. All electrical characterizations of 453

the transistors were performed using a parameter analyser (4200-SCS, Keithley) in vacuum 454

(≈10−3 Torr) at 170–350 K. No annealing was performed to avoid chemical interactions 455

between the materials and surface oxidation. 456

Material characterization. The spatial distribution of the conductive paths in the CBIC was 457

characterized via CAFM (NX-100, Park Systems). Current data were collected under a constant 458

bias of 1 V applied to the Pt-coated tip while keeping the CBIC grounded. AFM and KPFM 459

measurements were simultaneously performed with an NX-100 (Park Systems) in ambient 460

environment. To obtain the work function of the electrodes, the KPFM tip (Cr/Au-coated Si tip) 461

was calibrated using highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG), and differences in the contact 462

potential values between the tip and the electrode were measured. Cross-sectional STEM 463

images and EDS data were obtained using an aberration-corrected TEM (JEM-ARM200F, 464


<!-- Page 21 -->


21

JEOL) operated at 200 kV. Chemical identification of the samples was performed via XPS (PHI, 465

VersaProbe) with a micro-focused and monochromatic Al Kα (1,486.6 eV) excitation source. 466

Raman spectra were obtained using a micro-Raman spectrometer (LabRAM HR Evolution, 467

Horiba Jovin-Yvon) with a laser excitation wavelength of 532 nm. 468

Drift-diffusion simulations. Simulations of the photovoltaic devices were conducted using 469

SCAPS-1D software45. SCAPS is an open-source software and can be obtained from 470

https://users.elis.ugent.be/ELISgroups/solar/projects/scaps. The simulation parameters used in 471

this study are presented in Supplementary Table 3. 472

3D integral imaging. The size of the object used for the 3D imaging application was 473

approximately 15 mm × 15 mm. The scanning system consisted of an x-y planar linear stage 474

(VT-800, PI), a camera lens, a white light-emitting diode, and measurement units (Keysight 475

Technologies, B2901A). The camera lens was used to capture and focus the reflective image 476

on the photodiode. The source measurement unit measured the photocurrents of the photodiode. 477

All elemental images were acquired in reflection mode by illuminating the object with a white- 478

light source emitting approximately 1,000 lux. Finally, the full-colour 3D integral image was 479

obtained through the reconstruction process. During this process, the lens array had a focal 480

length of 22 mm and a sub-lens size of 19 mm. The display panel was a Lenovo Yoga 920 481

(3840(H) × 2160(V), 13.9” display with a pixel density of 317 PPI). 482
